sources.title: Texas judge grants restraining order against SEC, challenging ban on former pro athletes returning to college
sources.text:
The SEC faces its first challenge since voting to penalize coaches and schools that play former professional athletes. On Thursday, a Texas judge granted a collection of former college athletes temporary restraining orders against the NCAA, the SEC and commissioner Greg Sankey.
Earlier this week, the SEC unanimously voted to ban professional athletes from returning to college, and 15 of the 16 institutions voted to implement strict penalties on teams that defy that ban. LSU was the only school that abstained from the second vote.
Three athletes included in the latest Texas ruling -- receiver Jordan Hudson (Cowboys), linebacker Wesley Bissainthe (Chiefs) and receiver Omari Evans (Chiefs) -- are currently listed on NFL rosters.
This Texas lawsuit is the first to challenge the NCAA and SEC, but it won't be the last. According to Yahoo Sports , the Louisiana eligibility lawsuit has also been amended to include the SEC and Sankey. That suit includes three former Ole Miss players. Two of whom -- tight end Dae'Quan Wright and defensive tackle Xzavian Harris -- have already committed to LSU.
There was already some obvious tension between LSU and the SEC, and these lawsuits will only intensified it.
The SEC's penalty structure for playing former professional athletes, which was approved on Wednesday, includes a ban on the head coach for 50% of the season and a financial penalty equal to 50% of the sport's operation budget. Now that the temporary restraining order has been granted, the conference's ability to enforce it comes into question.
The Big Ten, ACC and Big 12 have also voted to impose tough penalties on teams that play former professional athletes, but to this point, the conferences haven't faced a legal challenge to its new policy.

sources.title: sec-tro-texas
sources.text:
We may still be more than a week out from the LSU Tigers playing college football, but there could already be an LSU vs. SEC battle brewing.
Naturally, at the center of it all are two LSU coaches, head football coach Lane Kiffin and Tiger basketball coach Will Wade. Kiffin signed former Cleveland Browns tight end and former Ole Miss player Dae'Quan Wright, as well as former Saints defensive tackle Zxavian Harris, also a former Rebel.
Their signings stem from a lawsuit filed in Louisiana state court, which opened the door for 16 former college football players, including Wright, to get a fifth year of eligibility.
Wade added former Big East Player of the Year RJ Luis to his roster, despite him signing contracts with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics' G League earlier this summer.
The Louisiana lawsuit is one of several filed as a result of the NCAA's eligibility rule change passed this summer, giving players five years of eligibility instead of the previous four. As a result, the SEC, along with other power conferences, have passed rules barring players who signed professional contracts from coming back to play in the NCAA.
Let's take a look at the showdown that might be brewing between Kiffin, Wade, the SEC and the players themselves.
This all got started last week. On August 19, a temporary restraining order was granted stemming from a lawsuit filed in a Louisiana state court, which paved the way for more than 30 plaintiffs to earn an additional year of eligibility.
The group includes several college football players, some of whom were on NFL rosters. The group included the aforementioned Harris and Wright, as well as former SMU running back TJ Harden, who played in Seattle's first preseason game before getting cut. The group also included former LSU linebacker Jack Plyburn, who is with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and former Notre Dame defensive end Junior Tuihalamaka.
Kiffin also added the former Fighting Irish defensive end, although Tuihalamaka was not on an NFL roster.
But earlier this week, the SEC took things a step further, passing a rule explicitly barring former professional players from re-joining SEC players.
Lane Kiffin is among the biggest supporters, naturally. I mean, who is surprised that the man who had one of the most dramatic exits in going from Ole Miss to LSU is at the center of this?
At a press conference earlier this week, Kiffin defended his signing of the players. He emphasized that if LSU didn't sign these players, another team would.
"At the end of the day, because of these rulings, they're either going to play for you or they're going to play for someone else around the country," Kiffin told reporters at a press conference . "So we've made the decision to recruit them like probably most people are."
He even further doubled down a day later, during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show."
"Over 100 athletes in multiple sports were cleared and said you could go play. That's a court order," Kiffin said via AL.com on Tuesday. "If you think back on all the different court orders of great players that were granted -- whether that's Diego Pavia or, now, Trinidad (Chambliss) that were allowed to play a sixth year, we followed all court orders. I think you get into a really interesting situation as a conference if you're now saying, 'Well, we're not going to follow this court order.' These kids that a court says can go anywhere, we're going to say, 'No you can't.'"
"This whole thing is ridiculous,: Landry said in a statement via Amanda Christovich of Front Office Sports . "Don't hate the player, hate the game. I've been saying for a year that college sports need to be fixed. The NCAA could have done it. Congress could have done it. Neither did.Now the SEC is creating a legal mess over athletes it told were out of eligibility, only to change the rules afterward.
"The SEC accepted the courts' decisions on Diego Pavia and Trinidad Chambliss. Why is this different? You can't tell athletes their college careers are over, watch them move on, change the rules later, and then punish them for not predicting the future."
Wade has also secured verbal commitments this offseason from former international professional players in Márcio Santos, Saliou Niang, Brice Dessert and Michael Ružić.
It appears that at least, for now, there could be a chance they do. Louisiana attorney Tony Clayton, who is representing several players in the state lawsuit, stated that the SEC's new rule change violates state law.
"The NCAA, in and of itself, are its member institutions," Clayton said via LouisianaSports.net . "So, the conferences cannot now circumvent the Louisiana law and say that they're going to issue a ban against these players when the courts have already ruled that the NCAA cannot do it.
"You can't camouflage yourself or act as some chameleon and say that you're something else, and you're going to come in and enforce the rule that the judge just said you could not."
The TRO allowing the 16 other players to play lasts just 10 days from the filing last week.
Clayton also later said that the complaint in the eligibility lawsuit was being amended to add the SEC and Greg Sankey, per Ross Dellenger.
Sankey asked Judge Ronald Johnson in East Baton Rouge Parish court to uphold NCAA rules that prevent athletes from returning, saying the decision is "essential to the integrity of college sports." He wrote that allowing pros back into NCAA competition would undermine the "fundamental principles" of college sports and unfairly harm high school students looking to join a college team as well as other teams that have followed the existing rules.
"These rules are grounded in the principle that athletics are an integral part of the academic experience," Sankey wrote. "The rules align the time permitted for college athletics with the pursuit of an undergraduate education and further the important purpose of preserving opportunities for future student-athletes to participate in college sports."
